Some preprint servers report being flooded with submissions. Credit: Michael Szebor/ Nature

In a bid to tackle the deluge of manuscripts it now receives, the preprint server arXiv has announced a cap of two papers per month for each submitting researcher, which began on 1 October.

The move follows a steep rise in submissions driven mainly by the slop generated by artificial-intelligence tools, says Steinn Sigurðsson, an astrophysicist at Pennsylvania State University in University Park and scientific director of arXiv. In September, 40,000 preprints were uploaded to arXiv, up from about 30,000 between March and July.

## Closing the floodgates

The cap is the latest measure introduced by arXiv to prevent its nearly 300 voluntary moderators from being completely overwhelmed by submissions, says Sigurðsson. They are now collectively checking about 1,000 manuscripts per day. This step is “holding up too many legitimate papers,” Sigurðsson says, noting that nearly 4,000 submissions are currently waiting to be posted on the site.

Some see the limit as entirely reasonable. Siddhesh Zādéy, an epidemiologist at Columbia University in New York City, says that it is not “stunting anyone's productivity”, because posting two preprint articles per month already requires a substantial amount of work.

Surge in fake citations uncovered by audit of 2.5 million biomedical-science papers

Others think that arXiv’s new policy should be stricter. Victor Galitski, a theoretical physicist at the University of Maryland in College Park, says that the limit can be circumvented by co-authors taking turns to submit studies.

Another preprint server, the social-sciences repository SocArXiv, now also restricts submissions to one article per author per week. “Sometimes there are good reasons to upload three papers at once, such as dissertation chapters,” notes Philip Cohen, a sociologist and demographer at the University of Maryland, who is director of SocArXiv. But most of the time, several submissions in rapid succession are “a good tip-off for AI slop”, he says.

Other venues are dealing with a rapid surge in submissions, and some major AI conferences and journals have turned to similar submission quotas .

## Clean up the literature

Some say that the issue of AI slop can’t be solved by rejecting more articles. “If arXiv turns those papers away, they’ll simply go somewhere else and become someone else’s problem,” says Natalie Khalil, the founder of Reviewer3 , a platform run from San Francisco, California, which uses AI to help researchers conduct peer review .

Artificial-intelligence systems such as large language models (LLMs) can exhibit behaviour that seems strikingly intelligent. This has led many people, including some experts, to wonder whether these systems could have some form of consciousness — the capacity for subjective experience. However, we think that existing AI systems are not conscious, and that, along current trajectories of development, they are not likely to become conscious. Greater clarity about whether AI could become consciousness will be crucial as society grapples with the challenges posed by this increasingly powerful technology.

Can AI ever be conscious? The question stems from a misconception

Several prominent scientists, including biologist Richard Dawkins and AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton, have argued that AI systems might already be conscious. And earlier this year, AI company Anthropic in San Francisco, California, published research claiming to have identified computational signatures of a form of consciousness in its Claude model 1 .

Whether AI models can ever be conscious is not merely a philosophical question. It has practical implications. For instance, if AI systems were conscious, they might experience distress and pain, similar to how people do. Then should countless new conscious entities that might experience suffering be allowed to proliferate? Perhaps not surprisingly, some people are already calling for ‘AI welfare’ and ‘AI rights’ to be taken seriously 2 .

Conversely, if AI systems only seem to be conscious and lack actual inner experience, then granting them rights or protections could hinder efforts to govern and control them at precisely the time when oversight is urgently needed. Following this path would draw attention and resources away from beings whose consciousness is not in any doubt.

Looking beyond humans and our closest relatives in the animal kingdom, it is still hard to be certain about what does, and does not, have the capacity for consciousness — be it insects, AI or the creations of synthetic biology, such as laboratory-grown brain organoids 3 , 4 .

Why we need mandatory safeguards for emotionally responsive AI

This uncertainty has prompted some researchers to advocate a precautionary approach: if there is a reasonable chance that AI systems could be conscious, then society must take anticipatory action and give those systems some form of protection against potential suffering. This, the argument goes, would avoid reprising moral errors of the past — for example, the mistreatment of non-human animals, or surgery on preterm human babies without anaesthesia. An extreme version of this idea is that society should reallocate resources from addressing the welfare concerns of present-day humans to lessen the potential suffering of trillions of future AI descendants.

In our view, uncertainty is not the same as knowing nothing, and it does not mean that all possibilities are equally likely to occur. Decisions about what is moral must weigh both the consequences of false negatives — failing to recognize consciousness where it exists — and the costs of false positives — attributing consciousness where none exists. In the case of AI, we think that false positives are much more likely to occur than false negatives are. If so, a precautionary approach would be misguided.

Between us, we’ve spent decades studying consciousness from diverse scientific perspectives: experimental neuroscience, theoretical neurobiology and philosophy of mind. On the basis of this work, we feel that consciousness in AI is extraordinarily unlikely, at least in the digital, silicon-based systems that underpin today’s technologies. Here, we set out three reasons for our scepticism.

## Intelligence is not consciousness

What we mean by consciousness is simple enough: it is what goes away with dreamless sleep or under general anaesthesia, and what returns after waking up or while dreaming. Conscious experiences feel like something, whether it is tasting ice cream on a hot day or seeing the vibrant colours of a sunset. Philosopher Thomas Nagel, whose influential 1974 essay ‘What is it like to be a bat?’ helped to shape modern debates about consciousness, arguing that a conscious organism is one for which there is “something that it is like to be that organism” 5 .

This definition of consciousness introduces the first reason for scepticism about conscious AI. Consciousness is not the same thing as intelligence. Consciousness is about being and feeling; intelligence — very broadly — is all about doing, or performing functions. Just because something is intelligent does not mean that it is conscious.

Humans know that we are conscious, and we tend to associate consciousness with using our intellectual capacities. Yet, conscious experience and intelligent behaviour can come apart in striking ways. We know firsthand that our brain and body can carry out highly intelligent processes wholly outside awareness. For example, the cerebellum adjusts and plans motor performance in a way that is precise, fast and adaptable through ongoing learning. Yet none of what it does involves consciousness directly — we are wholly unaware of all its ‘computations’. Moreover, absence or removal of the cerebellum, which contains nearly four-fifths of the neurons in the human brain, does not affect consciousness directly 6 .

AI is programmed to hijack human empathy — we must resist that

The temptation to conflate intelligence and consciousness probably reflects baked-in psychological biases — anthropocentrism, viewing the world through a human lens, and anthropomorphism, attributing human characteristics to things that merely resemble people. Consider, for example, the seductive power of language, a capacity that humans have long felt makes us special. When LLMs talk to us, it’s natural to project onto them properties that accompany our linguistic fluency, such as intelligence and consciousness.

But LLMs are trained on vast quantities of human-written text, much of it explicitly or implicitly concerned with thoughts, feelings and conscious experiences. LLMs are mirrors that reflect an image of our collective digitized past 7 . We gaze into them and all too readily confuse the reflections with our own conscious minds 8 .

The beguiling nature of LLMs is highlighted by considering the response to AlphaFold 9 , made by Google DeepMind in London. Similar to an LLM, AlphaFold is a powerful neural network running on silicon hardware. Yet almost nobody worries that it might be conscious. That’s because AlphaFold predicts protein structures, whereas LLMs ‘talk’ to us. The compelling illusion of consciousness created by linguistic fluency just isn’t there for AlphaFold.

## Silicon brains

Second, the idea of conscious AI is motivated by the assumption that algorithms running on silicon are, in principle, sufficient for consciousness 10 . In other words, that computation of the right kind is all that it takes, and that it doesn’t matter whether these computations are implemented inside carbon-based brains or in silicon-based computers. Philosophers call this assumption computational functionalism. Although computations are clearly sufficient to produce forms of intelligence — as modern AI systems demonstrate — it is much less clear that they could also be sufficient for consciousness.

Computational functionalism is widely assumed among members of the tech community and is popular among some scientists and philosophers, too, but we think it is fatally flawed because brains are not — or at least not just — computers that are made of meat.

## Abstract

Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have largely been driven by large language models, deep neural networks that operate over discrete units called tokens. To represent text, most large language models use words or word fragments as the tokens, known as subword tokenization 1 . Subword tokenization obscures fine-grained information, which is problematic, especially for scientific data—such as computer code or biological sequences—where meaning depends on the individual characters or bytes 2 . Models that instead operate directly on the byte encoding of text avoid these limitations, but until now they have lagged behind subword-based models in performance. Here we introduce a general method for creating byte-level large language models through byteification that approach the capabilities of subword-based systems. We use a two-stage conversion procedure to retrofit existing subword-based models into byte-level models with minimal extra training. The resulting models outperform earlier byte-level approaches and excel on character-level reasoning tasks, achieving practical inference speeds by efficiently processing byte-level information and adaptability by reusing the existing ecosystem around the source large language model. Our results remove a long-standing performance barrier to end-to-end byte-level language modelling, demonstrating that models operating on raw text encodings can scale competitively while offering advantages in domains requiring fine-grained textual understanding.

## Main

Recent progress in AI has been driven by end-to-end deep learning systems that learn representations directly from data. Large language models (LLMs) exemplify this trend, achieving strong capabilities by training on massive collections of text 3 , 4 . However, despite their apparent generality, contemporary LLMs are not fully end-to-end: before learning can begin, text must first be mapped to a sequence of discrete units called tokens. The choice of tokens, although sometimes overlooked, fundamentally shapes the representations that LLMs learn and the behaviours that they exhibit 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 .

The vast majority of contemporary LLMs use words or parts of words as the tokens in a process known as subword tokenization 1 , 10 . This leads to many problems. LLMs that use subword tokenization suffer from limited character-level understanding 11 , 12 , 13 , which especially hinders performance with scientific data, such as code and biological sequences 2 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ; they are also implicitly biased towards generating particular responses based on how the prompt is tokenized 18 , 19 , 20 , they are restricted in the number of words they can incorporate in their vocabulary, which in practice leads to English-centricity 6 , 21 , and they potentially suboptimally allocate their compute 2 , 22 . These problems have motivated extensive research into alternatives to subword tokenization, most commonly by using the underlying UTF-8 bytes that the text is encoded as 23 as the discrete units. Many earlier byte-level LLMs claim to outperform subword-level LLMs on the efficiency–performance Pareto frontier 2 , 22 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 . However, in practice, byte-level LLMs have not seen widespread adoption so far, and all leading LLMs still exclusively rely on subword tokenization.

We hypothesize that the key reason for this mismatch between theory and practice is that existing approaches to byte-level language modelling focus predominantly on training a new byte-level model from a random initialization and comparing it against a subword-level LLM also trained from a random initialization. By contrast, the training of state-of-the-art subword-level LLMs is rapidly evolving, combining innovations in training data curation, model architecture and post-training. Keeping up with this pace is infeasible for byte-level LLM development without extensive investments.

To resolve this mismatch, we introduce a general method for creating byte-level LLMs that achieve performance close to that of state-of-the-art subword-level LLMs across various tasks, while vastly surpassing earlier byte-level LLMs with a comparable parameter count. In contrast to earlier byte-level LLMs that focus predominantly on training from random initialization, we retrofitted an existing subword-level LLM to the byte level using less than 1% of a typical pretraining budget (49.1B tokens in total, where B represents a billion or 10 9 ). We refer to this process as byteification. Byteification establishes a connection between existing subword-level LLMs and byte-level LLMs. This let us train the byteified models Bolmo 7B and Bolmo 1B by starting from the existing fully open LLMs Olmo 3 7B 28 and OLMo 2 1B 29 , Bwen 8B by byteifying Qwen3 8B Base 30 , and Blama 8B by byteifying Llama 3 8B 31 .

Our architecture first aggregates the byte stream into a sequence of patches, where each patch itself consists of one or more bytes. The patches are then processed by a large transformer 32 language model and finally depooled into bytes. Owing to its latent tokenization into byte patches, we refer to this style of architecture as a latent tokenizer language model (LTLM). Examples of LTLMs include the DTP 24 , BLT 22 and H-Net 2 models. However, in contrast to earlier work, we specifically designed our architecture to be well suited to byteification (section ‘Byteified language model architecture’). In particular, we resolved a mismatch between the expressivity of subword tokenization and the latent LTLM tokenization. Alongside an efficient two-stage training procedure (section ‘Byteification training procedure’), this allowed us to quickly recover and, in some cases, surpass the performance of the source subword-level LLM. We believe that byteifying provides a key missing research direction by enabling the creation of state-of-the-art byte-level LLMs without extensive investment. This approach is complementary to training from random initialization. Making it cheap to byteify any subword model can quickly unveil high-performing architectures that are promising candidates for training from random initialization as byte-level LLMs.

Our byteified models outperformed, on average, all earlier publicly available byte-level LLMs of comparable size. For example, Bolmo 7B achieved a +16.5% absolute improvement in STEM tasks over BLT 7B, which was trained from random initialization. Bolmo 7B also greatly outperformed the source Olmo 3 on character understanding and was better in certain coding settings. Bwen 8B outperformed Bolmo 7B, exhibiting comparable trends and reaching performance close to and sometimes surpassing the source Qwen model. Furthermore, we found that the byteified models can arbitrarily be further sped up by training with higher ratios of bytes per patch, which is possible only to a limited extent in subword-level LLMs. Finally, we show that existing components in the source LLM ecosystem can be used to adapt a byteified model without any extra training cost; this could further accelerate research on byte-level LLMs.

In aggregate, our results show that byte-level LLMs offer substantial promise as a foundation for future language models, with potential advantages for computational efficiency by reducing energy and deployment costs, for reducing biases introduced by English-centric subword tokenization and for enabling applications that require fine-grained textual understanding, particularly in scientific and technical domains.

### Byteified language model architecture

Following the same overall structure as earlier LTLMs (‘Related work’ in Methods ), the byteified models can be formalized as shown in Fig. 1 . In a nutshell, a local encoder model operating over bytes first creates contextualized byte representations. A neural boundary predictor module then predicts, based on these representations, the byte positions at which to place a boundary. The boundary information is used to derive a sequence of patches: a patch is the contiguous sequence of bytes between consecutive boundaries (including the byte where the end boundary is placed). A pooling module then reduces the contextualized byte representations to a single representation per patch, which is passed through a deep global model. The patch representations contextualized through the global model are depooled back to the byte level and further contextualized through a local decoder model. Finally, the local decoder representations are used to predict the next byte and any other potential information. We chose the local models to be shallow but wide as we found that the embeddings of the original model typically have a high effective rank (Extended Data Fig. 1 ), and we chose matrix long short-term memory (mLSTM) layers 33 to contextualize local information as they retained high performance at high throughput in our experiments (Extended Data Fig. 3 ). See ‘Byteified model architecture details’ in Methods for a detailed description of the architecture. Our primary departure from earlier architectures lies in the non-causal patch boundary prediction. The boundary predictor of earlier LTLMs uses only the past context to decide on whether to place a boundary (it is causal, referred to as incremental by Pagnoni et al. 22 ). At a glance, this seems necessary: we are aiming to predict the next byte, so we must not leak any information about it. However, although subword-level LLMs use a causality constraint over the subword tokens, the subword tokens themselves do not depend exclusively on past context: subword tokenizers use information about future bytes to place token boundaries. To see this, let us interpret our subword tokenizer as a function that decides whether to place a token boundary after any byte: \({\mathcal{B}}(x):{\{0,1,\ldots ,255\}}^{n}\to {\{0,1\}}^{n}\) , where 1 at the n th place denotes a token boundary predicted after the n th byte. In other words, although the subword-level LLM uses only past subword tokens to predict the next subword token, the subword tokens themselves are created by taking future context into account. In this case, this means deciding that ‘ _Wor’ should be a token in one case but not in the other, although the text up until that point is equivalent.
